note: Clock times: per house rule the author's printed hour numbers are kept and only "o'clock" is translated — "six until six" / "six o'clock" -> "saa sita" (heading block 1 and block 2), "rose at five" -> "saa tano" (block 2), "a train to catch at four" -> "saa nne" (block 21). A native reviewer should note that in Swahili time-reckoning these read as midday/11am/10am; the English (European) hours are 6, 5 and 4. Durations ("twelve hours" -> "saa kumi na mbili") are durations, not clock times.

No Bible verse is quoted in this bio, so references is empty. Echoes only: "Only believe" / "amini tu" (blocks 0 and 6) is Wigglesworth's motto, echoing Mark 5:36 / Luke 8:50 — rendered "amini tu", which matches the SUV wording "Usiogope, amini tu" found in the shipped corpus. "Like Jeremiah ... a man with a fountain of tears" (block 9) echoes Jeremiah 9:1; his own words, rendered "chemchemi ya machozi", the SUV phrase. The heading "To the ends of the earth" (block 30) echoes Acts 1:8; rendered "Hata miisho ya dunia".
"the Lamb, the bleeding Lamb" is a hymn line, rendered "Mwana-Kondoo, Mwana-Kondoo anayetoka damu" (SUV form Mwana-Kondoo).

Book titles (Ever Increasing Faith, Faith That Prevails, Smith Wigglesworth: Apostle of Faith) kept in English as in the shipped Bosworth bio; the Frodsham title is glossed once in apposition ("— Mtume wa Imani —") because the next paragraph's "It is a fair title" depends on the reader understanding it.

Terminology follows f-f-bosworth.sw: "ubatizo katika Roho Mtakatifu", "uponyaji wa kiungu", "Kipentekoste", "kunena kwa lugha"; Salvation Army -> Jeshi la Wokovu; 'the Baptism' (Mary Boddy's word) kept capitalised as "Ubatizo"; Pentecost -> Pentekoste; appendicitis -> "ugonjwa wa kidole tumbo".

Place and institution names kept in English (West Riding, Bowland Street, St Peter's Church, All Saints', Glad Tidings Hall, Nab Wood Cemetery); country names use standard Swahili forms (Marekani, Uswisi, Norwei, Uswidi, Denmaki, Skandinavia, Afrika Kusini).
"went white with rage" rendered idiomatically as "nikigeuka rangi kwa hasira" (changing colour) rather than literally 'white'.
"He went on preaching into his late eighties" rendered "hadi umri wake ulipokaribia miaka tisini" (until his age approached ninety) — natural Swahili for 'late eighties'; consistent with death at 87.
